description: Short, practical guides that connect everyday decisions to evidence-reviewed cognitive-bias lenses.

entries.title: Why the First Price You See Changes What You Will Pay
entries.summary: A first price can quietly become a reference point, so a later price feels cheap or expensive in comparison instead of on its own.
entries.situation: You see a jacket for €300. A few minutes later it is marked down to €180. The second price suddenly feels attractive, even if you had never planned to spend €180 on a jacket.
entries.explanation: The first number gives your mind a starting point. When the next number arrives, you may judge it relative to that starting point instead of asking what the item is worth to you.
entries.whyItMatters: Anchors appear in discounts, salary talks, house prices and negotiations. They are especially easy to miss because the first number can shape the whole conversation before you have made your own estimate.
entries.tryThis: Before looking at the discount or seller's target, write down what you would pay based on your needs, alternatives and budget.
entries.takeaway: What would this be worth to me if I had not seen the first number?

entries.title: Why Bad Projects Are So Hard to Stop
entries.summary: Past effort can make a weak project feel too expensive to abandon, even when the next step no longer makes sense.
entries.situation: A team has worked on a product for eight months. Adoption is poor, but stopping now feels like wasting all that work. Another three months of funding starts to sound reasonable simply because so much has already been spent.
entries.explanation: Money and effort that are already gone cannot be recovered by continuing. The useful question is whether the next investment is attractive from today forward.
entries.whyItMatters: Projects, subscriptions, relationships with vendors and even personal plans can continue long after the original reason has disappeared. The more visible the past investment is, the harder it can feel to change direction.
entries.tryThis: Imagine the project arrived on your desk today with no history. Would you fund the next step with the information you have now?
entries.takeaway: If we had invested nothing yet, would we still choose the next step?

entries.title: Why We Keep Finding Evidence That We Are Right
entries.summary: Once we prefer an explanation, it becomes easy to search for supporting evidence and much harder to notice what could prove us wrong.
entries.situation: You think a new diet works. You search for success stories, save positive posts and remember friends who improved. Critical studies feel less convincing, so they receive less attention.
entries.explanation: A preferred belief can change what we search for, how we interpret mixed evidence and what we remember later. The result is a comfortable information loop.
entries.whyItMatters: Search engines and social feeds can make this easier because almost any view has supporting examples somewhere online. More searching does not automatically mean better checking.
entries.tryThis: Before searching, write one piece of evidence that would make you reduce confidence in your current view. Then actively look for the strongest version of that evidence.
entries.takeaway: What evidence would make me change my mind?

entries.title: Why Scary News Can Make Rare Events Feel Common
entries.summary: Vivid, emotional and repeated stories are easy to remember, and easy-to-remember events can feel more common than they really are.
entries.situation: After several dramatic reports about an accident, the risk suddenly feels much higher. You can picture the event clearly, while thousands of ordinary safe outcomes never became news.
entries.explanation: Our minds often use memorable examples as a shortcut when judging frequency or risk. A story can be memorable because it is recent or emotional, not because it is statistically typical.
entries.whyItMatters: This can affect travel, health worries, investing and public risk perception. Headlines naturally select unusual events, while base rates are usually much less exciting.
entries.tryThis: Keep the story, but add the denominator. Ask how often this event happens among all relevant cases, not only how many examples you can recall.
entries.takeaway: Is this easy to remember because it is common, or because it is vivid?

entries.title: Why Repeated Claims Start to Feel True
entries.summary: A claim can feel more believable after repeated exposure, even when the repetitions do not add new independent evidence.
entries.situation: You see the same claim in a video, a post, a newsletter and an AI answer. After the fourth encounter it feels familiar and therefore safer to accept.
entries.explanation: Familiar information is easier to process. That feeling of fluency can be mistaken for evidence, especially when several channels are repeating the same original source.
entries.whyItMatters: Repetition is cheap online. A weak claim can appear to have broad support when ten accounts, articles or generated answers all trace back to one source.
entries.tryThis: Trace an important claim back to independent sources. Count independent evidence, not the number of times you have seen the wording.
entries.takeaway: Did I verify this, or have I simply seen it many times?

entries.title: Why We Underestimate How Long Work Will Take
entries.summary: Detailed plans make the future feel controllable, but they often hide delays that similar projects have already taught us to expect.
entries.situation: A task looks like three clean steps, so the team estimates five days. Then access is late, a dependency breaks and review takes longer. Somehow the next project is estimated from another perfect plan.
entries.explanation: Planning from the inside focuses attention on how this project should unfold. Looking at comparable completed work gives an outside view of how projects actually unfold.
entries.whyItMatters: Small optimism in many tasks can create large delivery errors. Precise estimates also look more confident than ranges, which can make weak forecasts feel stronger than they are.
entries.tryThis: Before refining the plan, find three comparable completed tasks. Use their actual duration as the starting reference class, then explain why this case should differ.
entries.takeaway: What happened the last few times we did something similar?

entries.title: Why an AI's First Answer Can Shape Your Judgment
entries.summary: An AI estimate can become an anchor before you have formed your own view, making later reasoning orbit around the model's first number.
entries.situation: You ask an AI how long a migration should take and it answers six weeks. You then adjust the number to seven or eight weeks, but never build an estimate that is independent of the original six.
entries.explanation: The model's answer is now the starting point. Even careful adjustment can stay too close to that first value because the comparison has already been framed.
entries.whyItMatters: AI makes first estimates extremely easy to obtain. That is useful, but it also means an unverified number can enter a decision before anyone has checked a base rate, comparable case or constraint.
entries.tryThis: For important estimates, write your own range or reference class first. Then ask AI and compare the assumptions behind both numbers.
entries.takeaway: What would I estimate if I had not seen the AI's number first?

entries.title: Why Humanlike AI Can Feel More Trustworthy
entries.summary: Warm language, a name and a natural conversation can make software feel more understanding or reliable than its tested performance supports.
entries.situation: A chatbot remembers the tone of the conversation, apologises and explains an answer confidently. It starts to feel as if it understands the situation in the same way a person would.
entries.explanation: Humanlike cues make interaction easier, but they can also encourage us to infer human abilities, intentions or understanding that have not actually been tested.
entries.whyItMatters: A pleasant interface and a capable system are not the same thing. Trust should depend on what the system can access, verify and do reliably for the task.
entries.tryThis: Separate the interface from the capability. List what the AI would need to know or verify to support the answer, then check whether it really has that information.
entries.takeaway: Am I trusting the capability, or reacting to humanlike cues?

entries.title: Why a Good Result Does Not Always Mean a Good Decision
entries.summary: Luck can produce a good outcome from a weak process, while a strong decision can still end badly under uncertainty.
entries.situation: A manager makes a risky choice with little evidence and the project succeeds. Later the choice is praised as brilliant, even though the same process could easily have failed.
entries.explanation: Once the result is known, it is tempting to judge the earlier decision mainly through that result. But decision quality also depends on the information, alternatives and uncertainty available at the time.
entries.whyItMatters: Teams that reward outcomes without reviewing process can learn the wrong lesson. Lucky decisions may be repeated, while sensible decisions with unlucky outcomes may be abandoned.
entries.tryThis: Review the decision as if you did not know the outcome. Ask what information was available, what risks were considered and whether the process was reasonable.
entries.takeaway: Would I judge this decision the same way if the outcome were different?

entries.title: Why Past Events Feel Obvious After They Happen
entries.summary: Once we know the result, our memory of earlier uncertainty can shrink and the outcome starts to look easier to predict than it really was.
entries.situation: A product launch fails and everyone remembers the warning signs. A few months earlier, however, the team had several plausible scenarios and no clear agreement about which one would happen.
entries.explanation: Knowing the ending changes how earlier information looks. Signals that fit the outcome become more noticeable, while uncertainty and competing possibilities fade from memory.
entries.whyItMatters: This can create unfair blame and weak learning. If every result looks obvious afterward, we may believe future outcomes should also be easy to predict.
entries.tryThis: Keep short decision notes or forecasts before important outcomes. During the review, compare memory with what was actually written at the time.
entries.takeaway: What did I really expect before I knew the result?

entries.title: Why Today's Feelings Shape Choices for Your Future Self
entries.summary: It is easy to assume that your future preferences will look like your current mood, appetite or priorities.
entries.situation: You are exhausted after a difficult week and decide that you never want a demanding role again. A month later, after rest and a calmer schedule, the same career option feels very different.
entries.explanation: Your current state is real, but it may not be permanent. We can project today's preferences onto a future self who will have different energy, information and circumstances.
entries.whyItMatters: Long-term purchases, career decisions, schedules and commitments are often made in temporary states. Treating a temporary feeling as a permanent forecast can narrow options too early.
entries.tryThis: Name your current state before making a long-term choice. Then ask how the decision might look when you are rested, calm, busy or under different incentives.
entries.takeaway: Which part of today's state am I assuming will still be true later?

entries.title: Why Big Events May Change Us Less Than We Expect
entries.summary: When imagining a major future event, we often focus on that event and forget how much ordinary life will continue around it.
entries.situation: A promotion feels as if it will transform daily life. You picture the title, salary and celebration, but not the commute, laundry, meetings, family routines and normal frustrations that will still fill most weeks.
entries.explanation: A future event is vivid because it is the focus of the forecast. The rest of future life is less vivid, so we may overestimate how intense or long-lasting the emotional effect will be.
entries.whyItMatters: This does not mean major events are unimportant. It means forecasts can improve when the event is placed back inside an ordinary week rather than imagined in isolation.
entries.tryThis: Describe a normal Tuesday three months after the event. Include work, sleep, errands, relationships and the other things competing for attention.
entries.takeaway: Am I forecasting the event, or the whole life around it?
